archetype.name: Game Manager (short-area distributor)
archetype.definition: A veteran who wins by hitting the first open read underneath and between the numbers, and gets into trouble when asked to push the ball deep or carry a close game late.

report.headline: Accurate underneath, lost on third down and deep: a garbage-time-padded floor QB
report.take:
Brissett is what he has been for most of a decade: a big, sturdy, accurate-enough passer whose EPA lives near zero. His career rows show it. He has ranked mid-pack or worse in EPA per play in almost every season, with the 2019 and 2022 years as his best, and interceptions ranking near the bottom of the list more often than not. This year's -0.009 EPA per dropback (26th of 45) is not a collapse. It is his baseline, wrapped in a 221 yards-a-game volume line that a bad Arizona defense keeps propping up.

The passing profile splits sharply by depth. On short throws he completes 76.5% at +5.9 CPOE, and the intermediate window has been his best work: +0.458 EPA per attempt with no interceptions, mostly over the middle, where his throws carry +0.389 EPA. Beyond 20 air yards it falls apart: 18.2% completions, three of his six interceptions, -0.399 EPA. The notable change from 2025 is style. His time to throw dropped by 0.35 seconds and his aggressiveness (throws into tight windows) rose 7 points to 23.5%. His bad-throw rate actually improved to 11.5%, so the ball is cleaner, but he is forcing more of it. Week 4 against the Giants is the extreme case: 45.7% aggressive throws, three interceptions, -18.2 EPA.

The totals hide where the production comes from. Trailing by 9 or more, against defenses sitting on leads, he posts +0.205 EPA and +9.9 CPOE. In one-score games he is at -0.115 with five of his six picks. In close fourth quarters he is at -0.625. Third down is the worst of it: -0.383 EPA, a 31.4% conversion rate, four interceptions, and an average of 7.2 yards to go. That points to an offense that loses the down-and-distance battle and a quarterback who cannot bail it out. Arizona's 30th-ranked pass defense keeps putting him into the comfortable trailing script, which is why the volume stays respectable while the efficiency sags.

The trend is down. Over the last three games he is at -0.106 EPA per dropback with a 4.3% interception rate, both well off his season marks. The Rams win came without a touchdown pass. The good games came in shootouts (SF, DET) or when the opponent let him dink (Week 1). Expect the same shape going forward: a stable yardage floor from volume and short accuracy, touchdown upside only when the game gets away from Arizona, and a turnover rate that does not improve while the aggressiveness stays elevated.

strengths.title: Short and intermediate accuracy
strengths.body: Inside 20 air yards he places the ball well. He is +5.9 CPOE on short throws, and the 10-19 window has been the most efficient part of his game, with no interceptions. This fits his career and his quicker release this year, so it should hold. It is the engine of his yardage floor.

strengths.title: McBride and Bourne as reliable outlets
strengths.body: Trey McBride has drawn the most targets and returned +0.194 EPA per target. Kendrick Bourne has been even more efficient on lower volume. Both win in the short-to-intermediate areas he favors, so the connection is structural rather than lucky.

strengths.title: Avoids sacks for his release
strengths.body: His 4.9% sack rate ranks 12th and sits below the league average. It comes from the 2.59-second release more than from escapability, since his pressure-to-sack rate is ordinary. As long as he keeps getting the ball out, this holds.

concerns.title: Third down and close games
concerns.body: When the defense knows a pass is coming and the score is tight, his efficiency craters. He is at -0.383 EPA on third down, with a 31.4% conversion rate, and -0.625 in close fourth quarters. Long yardage-to-go is partly on the offense around him, but his career says this is a ceiling, not bad luck.

concerns.title: Deep ball and forced throws
concerns.body: Deep attempts have produced three interceptions and an 18.2% completion rate. The 7-point jump in aggressiveness from last year has turned into more picks without more big plays. On 22 deep attempts the sample is small, but the interception rate has climbed in recent weeks rather than settling.

concerns.title: Production padded by trailing scripts
concerns.body: His best numbers come when Arizona is down 9 or more, while one-score games drag his EPA well below zero. The team's 30th-ranked pass defense makes this likely to continue. Read that as volume he can count on, not as a sign he is better than his baseline.

trend.note: Weeks 1 and 3 were his best. Since then the Giants' three-interception game and a touchdown-less win over the Rams have pulled him to -0.106 EPA per dropback over the last three, with the Lions shootout the lone volume spike.

nextGame.headline: Top-three pass defense, minus Surtain and Hufanga, invites a tight game
nextGame.body:
Denver ranks 3rd in pass EPA allowed, 3rd in hit rate and 6th against deep throws. That shuts off the part of his game that already does not work and puts heat on a quarterback whose pressure-to-sack rate is only average. The opening is underneath: Denver ranks 20th on short passes, and the tight end has found room (TE1 EPA per play ranks 27th). That suits a McBride-heavy short game. Offenses also lean toward the run against them, and their 26th-ranked run defense makes a ground-first plan likely. That could cap his attempts. Denver's offense ranks 24th, so a blowout that sends him into his comfortable trailing script is less likely than a one-score grind, which is his weakest game state.

Availability cuts both ways. Denver is without CB Pat Surtain II and S Talanoa Hufanga, both everyday starters. That weakens the secondary meaningfully and is the main reason this is not a worse spot. On his side, Jeremiyah Love (ankle) is listed Out but reportedly set to do some running this week, and James Conner remains on IR. If Love sits, Tyler Allgeier leads the backfield, and Allgeier has been a weak receiving outlet at -0.241 EPA per target.

keyMatchups.title: McBride against Denver's soft middle
keyMatchups.body: Denver gives up its weakest coverage numbers on short throws and to tight ends by EPA per play. McBride is Brissett's most dependable target, so this is where completions will come from. One caution: tight ends have still scored below their averages against Denver in PPR, so the efficiency may not turn into big lines.

keyMatchups.title: Denver's pass rush
keyMatchups.body: Denver hits quarterbacks at a top-three rate. Brissett's protection is middle of the pack, and he has taken 12 sacks. His quick release is the counter. If Denver wins early downs, his third-down struggles will compound.

keyMatchups.title: Run-funnel script
keyMatchups.body: Offenses pass less than usual against Denver, which is soft on the ground. That plus a 43.5 total points to a lower-volume, close game, the setting where Brissett's EPA is worst.

nextGame.watch: Whether Arizona keeps the game close: a one-score fourth quarter means his worst splits decide it.

restOfSeason.body:
The yardage floor is real. He throws 39 times a game behind a defense that keeps falling behind, and his short accuracy has held for years. Touchdowns should stay around his career norm, and they depend on shootout weeks like Detroit and San Francisco. The interception rate is the piece most likely to stay ugly while he keeps throwing into tight windows at this rate, though the deep-ball picks come from a small sample and could ease. Expect a projection of about 200-240 passing yards a game, roughly 1.1-1.7 touchdowns, and interceptions near one a game. Efficiency should hover around league average or slightly below, which matches his career.

The upside case needs the team defense to stay bad, which keeps him throwing in trailing scripts, and Love returning to give the offense better early-down footing. The downside is a run of close, low-total games against good pass defenses, where his third-down and late-game numbers take over.
swingFactors: How often Arizona's defense forces trailing scripts
Whether his aggressiveness and interception rate settle

confidence.note: Six starts, but his profile matches a long, consistent career baseline; game-script splits are noisier.
